learningObjective: Explain why GEMV is memory-bound on GPU and how per-row parallelism does not change its roofline classification.

canonicalClaims.claim: GEMV has arithmetic intensity ~1 flop/byte for FP16 (2 flops per FMA over M*N bytes of A streaming), well below the ridge point of modern GPUs; runtime is bandwidth-limited by streaming A.
conditions: A is [M, N] and not cache-resident (M*N far exceeds L2).
The kernel does not artificially reuse A across many GEMVs (which would turn it into batched GEMM).
nonImplications: Does not imply that GEMV can never use tensor cores.
Does not imply that quantizing weights automatically speeds up GEMV without a compatible dequant kernel.

misconceptions.claim: GEMV is compute-bound when N is large.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both flops and bytes scale linearly in N; the ratio (intensity) is constant, not growing.

misconceptions.claim: GEMV bottleneck is the log(N) reduction depth on each row.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The reduction is trivially parallel and short; the streaming HBM read of A dominates wall time.

misconceptions.claim: Using tensor cores automatically turns GEMV compute-bound.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Tensor cores raise peak flops but do not change intensity or HBM bandwidth; a bandwidth-bound kernel remains bandwidth-bound.

implementationFacts: Typical GEMV kernel: one warp or CTA per row; use warp-shuffle for the inner reduction.
Weight-only INT4 quantization is popular for LLM decode because it cuts A bandwidth ~4x.
performanceScenarios: LLM decode step per layer is essentially a batch-1 GEMV per weight matrix; memory bandwidth of weights dominates.
